question: While the EU has been a strong supporter of international conventions banning the use, production, stockpiling, and transfer of anti-personnel landmines (Ottawa Convention1) and cluster munitions, several Member States have recently withdrawn or announced their intentions to withdraw from these treaties. The EU is a major donor in mine action, providing substantial aid for mine clearance worldwide.

On 14 April 2025, Council Decision 2025/7812 was adopted to further support the implementation and universalisation of the Ottawa Convention. On 23 October 2025, the EU delegation to the UN declared before the First Committee on Disarmament: ‘We are deeply concerned by the ongoing use of anti-personnel mines.
The EU is resolute in its support for and advancing of the humanitarian objectives of the [Ottawa] Convention, which remains [...] an important and effective humanitarian disarmament instrument.

’ Yet, according to Security Action for Europe Regulation (SAFE), simplified and accelerated common procurement procedures will now be established for the acquisition of products for defence purposes, including military counter mobility, a category that includes barriers and obstacles intended to restrict enemy movement, which could encompass landmines. Against this backdrop, can the Commission clarify: 1.
If SAFE funding for the procurement and use of landmines will be allowed?
And if so, whether that would be contrary to its public position and a violation of the EU treaties and international humanitarian law?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.3.2026) The Security Action for Europe (SAFE) Regulation1 provides financial assistance to Member States for the acquisition of defence products or other products for defence purposes belonging to categories laid down in the Regulation, including counter mobility.

The Regulation makes also reference to applicable international law prohibiting the use, development or production of specific defence products. This is because the Regulation does not affect the rules of international law which prevail.

The international conventions on prohibited weapons such as the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention (Ottawa Convention) are ratified by Member States and are binding upon them, rather than upon the EU. Member States must thus use the SAFE loans in respect with these binding conventions.

Moreover, Articles 3(5) and 21 of the Treaty on the European Union2 expressly refer to the EU obligation to respect international law. International Humanitarian Law applies in all situations, including those of armed conflict as it is primarily intended to protect civilians, humanitarian personnel and victims of such conflicts.

The EU will continue to support and pursue the objectives of the Ottawa Convention in line with established policies. The withdrawing Member States remain committed to the humanitarian goals of the Convention and bound by their obligations pursuant to International Humanitarian Law, in all circumstances and regardless of the behaviour of the adversary.
